mechanism: A memory map is an index file that lists the paths an agent is told to read. A nightly script parses the paths out of the index, checks each exists on disk (and optionally that the file is non-empty and was touched within a set age), and reports the dead ones. It depends only on a parseable index format and the filesystem, so it needs no model.

idea_why: Stale index entries fail silently, and an existence check is cheap and deterministic.

Report missing, empty and old files to a log, and have the nightly runner append the count. Add a second check that every file in the folder is listed in the index, to catch orphans. No hire needed.

mechanism: Coding agents fan out parallel sub-agents, so several requests hit the local model at once. Ollama by default queues requests and answers them one at a time, while servers with continuous batching (LM Studio's MLX engine, llama.cpp server with parallel slots, vllm-mlx style servers) serve them together. Single-request tokens per second, which most comparisons report, hides this difference.
claim: Popular Ollama versus LM Studio comparisons measure single-request speed, not concurrent sub-agent load, which is where the real gap is.
why_not_testable: Needs a local model runtime, and there is no local LLM on this Mac.
needs: A local LLM server (Ollama or LM Studio) and a model download.
one_line: Local models stall under Claude Code because Ollama serves parallel sub-agent requests one by one; batching servers do not.
idea_why: Serial queueing against parallel clients is a well understood mechanism, and the benchmark framing point holds.
breakdown: Install a batching server, load one small model, fire four simultaneous requests from a Python script and time wall-clock against four sequential ones. Repeat on Ollama with and without its parallel setting. The data is a ratio of total time, which is easy to read.
